script: Good morning and welcome to the Saltworks Heritage Centre. I'm Maeve, and I'll be showing you round today.
The tour takes about an hour. Photographs are welcome everywhere except in the archive room, where the flash can damage old documents.
Salt was produced on this site for nearly three hundred years. Many visitors imagine it was dug out of the ground, as in a mine, but here it was made by boiling seawater in large, shallow iron pans.
The pans were heated by coal fires. In fact, the works was built here because coal could be brought in cheaply by canal, not because the sea here is especially salty.
Our first stop is the boiling house. The original pans were sold as scrap in the nineteen-twenties, so what you'll see are replicas, built by local volunteers using old photographs.
Next we'll visit the workers' room. Life was hard here: the heat and steam were constant, and workers were often paid partly in salt rather than in coins.
Children worked here too. Their main job was not carrying salt, as people often think, but raking the crystals towards the edges of the pans.
After that comes the packing store. Salt was pressed into blocks, wrapped in paper and stamped with the company's symbol, a seagull, so that customers could recognise it.
The works finally closed in nineteen fifty-one. The main reason was competition from cheaper rock salt, brought by railway from inland mines.
Today the centre is run by a charity. Ticket money covers about half our costs; the rest comes from the café and the gift shop.
Speaking of the shop, the most popular item there is not the salt itself, but the small hand-painted salt boxes made by a local potter.
Finally, the floor in the boiling house can be uneven, so please watch your step. Right, let's begin.

paragraphs: A. Few substances are as ordinary, or as historically significant, as common salt. Today it sits in a shaker on almost every kitchen table and costs very little, yet for most of human history it was a valuable commodity, fought over, taxed and traded across vast distances. The reason is simple: before refrigeration, salt was one of the only reliable ways to preserve food, allowing communities to store meat and fish through the winter and to supply armies and sailors on long journeys.

B. Salt preserves food by drawing water out of it. Bacteria and moulds need moisture to grow, so when salt is rubbed into meat or used to make a strong brine, most of these organisms cannot survive. Archaeologists have found evidence of salt production in China dating back more than four thousand years, and in Europe early salt workers boiled brine from natural springs in clay pots, which they then broke to remove the solid salt. Large mounds of broken pottery still mark many of these sites.

C. Because salt was essential, it became a convenient target for governments in need of money. In ancient China, the state controlled salt production for long periods, and the revenue helped to fund armies and public works. In France, a hated salt tax known as the gabelle was charged for centuries; it varied enormously from one region to another, which encouraged widespread smuggling. Some historians list resentment of the tax among the many grievances that contributed to the French Revolution, although it was certainly not the only cause.

D. Salt also shaped the map. Roads were built to carry it from coasts and mines to inland markets, and a number of towns grew up at important points along these routes. In Africa, caravans crossed the Sahara carrying slabs of rock salt southwards, where it was exchanged for gold and other goods. It is often claimed that Roman soldiers were paid entirely in salt, giving English the word 'salary'. Historians now treat this story with caution: the word is certainly connected to salt, but there is little direct evidence that soldiers received their wages in this form.

E. The industrial age transformed salt from a scarce resource into a cheap one. New drilling techniques allowed producers to reach deep underground deposits, and pumping water into these deposits to dissolve the salt became common. At the same time, refrigeration reduced the need for salt as a preservative. Yet demand did not fall. Instead, most of the salt produced today is not eaten at all; it is used by the chemical industry, to make products such as plastics and glass, or spread on roads to melt ice in winter.

F. In recent decades, attention has shifted towards health. Doctors have long warned that eating too much salt is linked to high blood pressure, and many countries now encourage food manufacturers to reduce the amount they add to processed products. Interestingly, studies suggest that most of the salt people consume comes not from the shaker but from bread, ready meals and other packaged foods, which means that individual choices at the table make only a limited difference.

G. Meanwhile, a small revival of traditional methods is under way. Artisan producers on coasts from Brittany to Japan harvest sea salt by hand, letting the sun and wind evaporate seawater in shallow ponds. Their product can cost many times more than ordinary table salt, and supporters praise its texture and flavour. Critics point out that, chemically, the differences are small. Even so, the trend shows how a substance once so precious that it was guarded and taxed continues to carry cultural meaning far beyond its price.

script: Good evening. On tonight's programme I want to talk about something many listeners have written in about: learning a new language as an adult.

Let's start with a popular belief, that adults simply can't learn languages as well as children. Research gives a more mixed picture. Children usually end up with a more native-like accent, but adults often make faster progress at the start, because they're better at understanding grammar rules.
So what helps? The first tip from our experts is not to buy expensive software, but to set a realistic daily routine. Fifteen minutes every day, they say, beats two hours once a week.

The second tip is about mistakes. Many adult learners are afraid of sounding foolish, so they avoid speaking. Teachers say this fear, rather than a poor memory, is the biggest barrier for most adults.
One listener, Hannah, wrote to tell us how she learned Italian in her sixties. She said that what made the difference wasn't classes or apps, but joining a choir that sang Italian songs.
Singing, it seems, helps with pronunciation and rhythm, and the words stay in your memory for longer.

Another listener asked whether it's worth learning a language that only a few million people speak. Our panel was clear: smaller languages often open doors, because speakers are so pleased when outsiders make the effort.
Now, accents. Some learners worry a great deal about their accent. Most experts feel this matters far less than pronouncing individual sounds clearly. Being understood is the real goal.
What about watching films? Experts recommend it, but with subtitles in the language you're learning, not in your own language. That way, you link the sounds to the written words.
Finally, motivation. Our experts say the learners who keep going longest are those with a personal reason, such as family or travel, rather than those learning only for an exam.
That's all for tonight. Next week: how bilingual children switch between languages.

paragraphs: A. Every speaker has an accent. The term simply describes the way a person pronounces a language, and it reflects where they grew up, the people they spent time with and, to some extent, the social groups they wish to belong to. Although people often talk about someone 'having no accent', linguists point out that this is impossible. What people usually mean is that a speaker's accent matches the one they themselves consider normal or prestigious.

B. Accents are not fixed. Recordings made over the past century show that the pronunciation of many languages has shifted noticeably within living memory. In English, for example, early radio announcers sound strikingly formal to modern listeners, partly because certain vowels have moved since then. In one study, researchers compared broadcasts made by a long-serving newsreader over thirty years and found that her vowels had gradually moved closer to those of her younger listeners, even though she had never consciously tried to change the way she spoke.

C. One of the strongest forces behind change is contact between groups. When people move to cities, they encounter many different ways of speaking, and over time new mixed accents can develop. Linguists describe a process called levelling, in which the most unusual local features fade while features shared by many speakers survive. As a result, the accents of young people in large cities are often more similar to each other than those of their grandparents were. Similar processes have been observed in new towns built in the twentieth century, where the children of families from many different regions developed a shared local accent within a single generation.

D. Contrary to popular belief, television and the internet appear to play a smaller role than face-to-face conversation. People rarely pick up pronunciation simply by listening to broadcasts; they adapt most when they are talking directly to others, especially friends and peers. Several studies have found that new words from popular programmes spread quickly through a population, while the sounds of speech change much more slowly.

E. Adolescence is a particularly important period. Teenagers often lead changes in pronunciation, partly because they spend so much time with friends of the same age and partly because speech is one way of showing identity. Once people reach their twenties, their accents tend to become more stable, although they never stop changing entirely. Adults who move to a new region frequently adopt some local features, especially if they intend to stay for a long time.

F. Attitudes to accents can have real consequences. Surveys in several countries have found that listeners make quick judgements about a speaker's intelligence, friendliness or trustworthiness on the basis of accent alone. In experiments using recorded job interviews, candidates with accents seen as 'standard' have sometimes been rated more highly, even when their answers were identical to those of other candidates. Such findings have led some employers to train interviewers to recognise this kind of bias. Researchers stress, however, that such reactions are learned rather than natural, and that they vary greatly from one country to another.

G. Despite these pressures, regional accents remain remarkably resilient. Many speakers value their accent as a link to their home and community, and some even exaggerate local features when they return home after a period away. For linguists, this tension between change and loyalty is what makes accents so fascinating: they are at once deeply personal and constantly in motion. Some researchers add that new working habits may yet alter this picture: as more people spend their days in online meetings with colleagues from many regions, the balance between local and wider influences could shift in ways that are not yet understood.

script: Hello, everyone, and thank you for volunteering at the Lakeside Museum. I'm Ruth, the volunteer coordinator.
Let me start with shifts. Most volunteers work one four-hour shift a week. You can choose mornings or afternoons, but we ask you to commit for at least six months, because training takes time.

The museum holds around forty thousand objects, but only about five per cent are on display at any one time. The rest are kept in the store, which is temperature-controlled.
In the store, you must wear cotton gloves when handling most items. The exception is glass and ceramics. For those we use clean, bare hands, because gloves can make them slip.
For visitors, the most popular gallery isn't the dinosaurs, as you might guess, but the old toy collection. Adults love seeing the toys they played with as children.

paragraphs: A. Visitors to a large museum may spend hours walking through its galleries, yet they see only a small fraction of what the institution owns. In many national museums, fewer than one in ten objects is on display at any time. The rest are kept in storage rooms, sometimes in the same building but increasingly in purpose-built warehouses on the edge of the city. To some critics this seems wasteful, even a kind of hoarding. Others see it simply as a sign of poor planning. Museum professionals, however, argue that storage is central to what museums do.

B. One reason is space. Galleries need room for people to move, read labels and look at objects from different angles, and a crowded display quickly becomes tiring. Many objects are also too fragile to be shown for long. Textiles, watercolours and early photographs fade when exposed to light, so curators often display them for a few months and then return them to darkness to rest for several years. Light levels in galleries are therefore carefully controlled, and some displays are kept deliberately dim, which visitors occasionally mistake for poor design.

C. Storage collections are also used for research. Scientists studying climate change, for example, have examined bird specimens collected more than a century ago to measure changes in body size, while plant collections have helped to track when species first arrived in new regions. Such work depends on large numbers of similar objects, which would never be displayed side by side but which are extremely valuable as a set. Similar collections of insects have been used to study the decline of pollinators, and old seed samples have even been grown again to recover plant varieties that had disappeared from farms.

D. Keeping these collections safe is expensive. Stores must be protected from damp, pests and sudden changes in temperature, and every object needs to be recorded so that it can be found again. In the past, records were kept on handwritten cards, and some museums still hold objects whose origin is uncertain because the cards were lost or damaged. Digitising these records is a slow process: a single large museum may need decades to photograph and describe its entire collection. Climate-controlled buildings also consume large amounts of energy, which has led some institutions to experiment with more natural methods of regulating humidity.

E. Some museums have responded to criticism by opening their stores to the public. Visible storage, in which objects are kept in glass-fronted cabinets that visitors can walk past, has become popular in Scandinavia and the Netherlands. A few institutions now offer guided tours of their warehouses, where visitors can watch conservators at work. Surveys suggest that such tours appeal particularly to repeat visitors who feel they have already seen the main galleries.

F. Another response has been to lend objects more widely. Rather than leaving items in storage, larger museums increasingly lend them to smaller regional museums, schools and even hospitals. Lending involves its own risks, since objects must be packed, transported and insured, but supporters argue that the benefits for local communities outweigh these costs. Digital technology offers a further option: detailed three-dimensional scans allow people anywhere in the world to examine objects online, although few researchers believe that a scan can fully replace the experience of studying the real thing.

G. Finally, there are difficult questions about whether museums should simply collect less. Some curators now argue that collections should be reviewed regularly, and that duplicate or badly damaged objects could be transferred to other institutions or, in rare cases, disposed of. This idea remains controversial, because objects that seem unimportant today may prove valuable to researchers in the future, as the bird specimens demonstrate.

script: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Reef Discovery Centre. My name's Joel, and I'm one of the marine biologists here.
Most people think of coral as a kind of plant, or perhaps a rock. In fact, each coral is made up of tiny animals called polyps, which build hard skeletons around themselves.
Many corals get most of their food from microscopic algae that live inside their tissues. The algae also give the coral its colour.
When the water becomes too warm, the coral pushes out these algae and turns white. That's what we call bleaching. A bleached coral isn't dead yet, but if the heat lasts for weeks, it may starve.
Here at the centre, our main project is growing coral fragments in underwater nurseries and then planting them back on damaged reefs.
We look especially for fragments from corals that survived the last heatwave, because they may cope better with future warming.
Surprisingly, our biggest challenge isn't funding, but finding enough trained divers to do the planting.
That's why we run a volunteer diving programme. To take part you need an advanced diving certificate, but you don't need any scientific background.
In the next room you'll see our tanks. The largest holds around two hundred fish, but the star attraction is a small octopus called Inky, who has learned to open jars.
Feeding takes place at three o'clock every day, and children are welcome to help, as long as an adult is with them.
Before you leave, do look at our map wall, where visitors can pin a note about how they'll protect the ocean at home.

paragraphs: A. Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all known marine species. They protect coastlines from waves, supply fish to hundreds of millions of people and attract tourists whose spending supports entire regional economies. Because of this, the health of reefs has become one of the most closely watched indicators of how the oceans are responding to climate change, and reports of their decline regularly make headlines around the world.

B. The main threat is heat. Reef-building corals live in a partnership with tiny algae that provide them with most of their energy through photosynthesis. When sea temperatures rise just one or two degrees above their usual summer maximum for several weeks, this partnership breaks down. The coral expels the algae and loses its colour, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures fall quickly, the algae can return and the coral may recover; if not, the coral may die, leaving a skeleton that is soon covered by seaweed.

C. Mass bleaching events, in which reefs across whole regions bleach at the same time, were almost unknown before the 1980s. Since then they have become more frequent, and the gaps between them have shortened. This matters because a badly damaged reef typically needs a decade or more to recover, and if serious heatwaves arrive every few years, recovery is repeatedly interrupted. Some reefs that were once dominated by complex branching corals are now covered mainly by simpler, slower-growing species. Fish that depend on these complex structures for shelter often decline as a result.

D. Heat is not the only problem. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, its water becomes slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons. Pollution from farms, sediment from construction and damage from destructive fishing all add further stress. In some regions, outbreaks of coral-eating starfish, encouraged by nutrients washed from the land, have destroyed large areas of reef within a few years. Scientists stress that reefs already weakened by these local pressures are generally less able to survive heatwaves than reefs in cleaner, better protected waters.

E. Not all the news is bad. Some corals appear to tolerate heat better than others, and in certain locations reefs have recovered faster than expected. Researchers are investigating whether these tougher corals could be bred and planted on damaged reefs. Others are testing ways to shade reefs during heatwaves, for example by spraying a fine mist of seawater above the surface to reflect sunlight. Such techniques, however, are expensive and can only be used over small areas, so they are unlikely to protect more than a tiny fraction of the world's reefs.

F. Local communities are also taking action. In parts of the Pacific and the Caribbean, fishing groups have agreed to close sections of reef for several years so that fish populations can recover. Where these closures have been respected, numbers of plant-eating fish have increased, and these fish help reefs by grazing on seaweed that would otherwise smother young corals. Such schemes tend to succeed when local people help to design the rules, rather than having them imposed from outside.

G. Most marine scientists agree that efforts of this kind can buy time but cannot by themselves save reefs. The long-term future of coral depends above all on limiting global warming. Even so, protecting reefs from local damage remains worthwhile, because healthier reefs have a better chance of surviving until, as many hope, ocean temperatures eventually stabilise. Many also argue that reef protection and climate action should not be seen as alternatives: both are needed, and progress on one makes the other more effective.

script: Hi, everyone. I'm Dr Lena Brooks, and I'm a podiatrist, which means a foot specialist. Tonight I'll give you some practical advice on footwear for walking.
First, when should you buy shoes? Feet swell during the day, so the best time to try shoes on is in the late afternoon, not first thing in the morning.
Always try shoes on with the socks you'll actually walk in. Thick walking socks can make a surprising difference to the fit.
There should be about a thumb's width of space between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. And remember, your longest toe isn't always your big toe.
Many people assume they need heavy leather boots for country walks. For most paths, though, light walking shoes are perfectly adequate, and they're less tiring.
Boots are worth it mainly if you'll be carrying a heavy pack, or walking on rough, rocky ground.
How long do shoes last? A common rule is about eight hundred kilometres. The outside may still look fine, but the cushioning inside wears out.
New shoes need breaking in. Wear them around the house first, then on short walks, before any long trip.
One of the commonest problems I see is blisters. These are usually caused not by the shoe itself but by moisture, so socks made of wool or synthetic material are better than cotton.
Finally, a word on children. Children's feet grow quickly, and they should have their feet measured about every three months.
Handing down shoes from older brothers and sisters isn't ideal either, because shoes gradually take the shape of the first wearer's foot.

paragraphs: A. Humans have walked on two legs for millions of years, but for most of that time they did so barefoot. The oldest surviving shoes are sandals made of woven plant fibres, found in caves in North America and dated to around ten thousand years ago. Indirect evidence suggests that footwear is older still. Some researchers argue that the small toe bones of people living around forty thousand years ago were weaker than those of earlier humans, a change that would be expected if feet were regularly protected rather than gripping the ground directly.

B. Early shoes served practical purposes. In cold regions, wrapping the feet in animal skins prevented frostbite, while in hot deserts sandals protected the soles from burning sand and sharp stones. A remarkably well-preserved leather shoe found in a cave in Armenia, more than five thousand years old, was stuffed with grass, which may have been used for warmth or to help the shoe keep its shape when it was not being worn. In some cultures, shoes were removed before entering homes or sacred places, a custom that survives widely today.

C. Over time, shoes became markers of status as much as tools. In several societies, laws once controlled who could wear particular colours or styles. Extremely long, pointed toes became fashionable among wealthy men in medieval Europe, and in some places the permitted length of the point was officially linked to the wearer's rank. High heels, now associated mainly with women's fashion, were originally worn by horse riders, because a heel helped to keep the foot in the stirrup.

D. Until the nineteenth century, most shoes were made by hand, one pair at a time, and shoemakers often did not distinguish between the left and right foot; customers simply wore a pair until each shoe had adapted to its foot. The introduction of sewing machines and standard sizes transformed the industry, making footwear far cheaper. Mass production also meant that styles which had once been limited to the rich spread rapidly through the population. By the early twentieth century, a single factory could produce thousands of pairs a day.

E. The modern trainer emerged from a combination of rubber technology and the growing popularity of sport. Rubber soles, which became practical after new processing methods were developed, were quieter and more flexible than leather, and early canvas sports shoes were sold mainly for tennis. From the 1970s onwards, the rise of jogging created demand for shoes with thick cushioning, and running shoes became a symbol of a healthy lifestyle as well as a piece of sports equipment.

F. In recent years, some scientists have questioned whether heavily cushioned shoes are always beneficial. Studies of people who have grown up barefoot show that they tend to land on the front or middle of the foot when running, rather than on the heel. Supporters of minimalist footwear claim that this style reduces injuries, but the research so far is mixed, and switching suddenly to thin-soled shoes can itself cause problems, particularly in the calf muscles. Most specialists therefore advise runners who want to try such shoes to make the change gradually, over several months.

G. Footwear also has a significant environmental cost. Billions of pairs are made every year, most of them from materials that are difficult to recycle because rubber, plastics and textiles are glued together. Several manufacturers are now experimenting with designs that can be taken apart at the end of their life, or with soles made from plant-based materials, though such shoes remain a small part of the market and often cost more than conventional ones. Some brands also offer repair services, encouraging customers to replace worn soles instead of buying new pairs.

paragraphs: A. For centuries, a handful of plants grown in a few tropical regions shaped the economies of distant continents. Pepper from southern India, cinnamon from Sri Lanka, and nutmeg and cloves from a small group of islands in what is now eastern Indonesia were carried thousands of kilometres to markets in the Middle East, Africa and Europe. Their value came partly from their flavour and partly from their rarity: for a long time, the plants simply could not be grown anywhere else, and their sources were jealously guarded by the merchants who controlled them.

B. Contrary to a popular myth, spices were not mainly used to hide the taste of rotten meat. Historians point out that people who could afford expensive spices could generally also afford fresh food. Instead, spices were prized as signs of wealth and sophistication, and they were widely used in medicine, perfume and religious ceremonies as well as in cooking. Recipe collections from wealthy households show that spices were added generously to sweet as well as savoury dishes.

C. For much of history, the trade was organised as a chain of intermediaries. Growers sold to local merchants, who sold to traders sailing across the Indian Ocean, who in turn sold to merchants in ports such as Alexandria. Each step added to the price, so that by the time pepper reached northern Europe it might cost many times what it had at its origin. European consumers usually had little idea where these products actually came from, and colourful stories about dangerous creatures guarding the plants helped to keep prices high.

D. The desire to bypass these intermediaries was one of the forces behind European voyages of exploration in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. When Portuguese ships reached India by sailing around Africa, they opened a direct sea route. Within a century, Dutch and English trading companies were competing fiercely for control of the spice islands, and their conflicts were often violent. On some islands, local populations suffered terribly as foreign powers tried to establish monopolies over production. The voyages were extremely risky, and many ships and sailors never returned, but a single successful cargo could make investors very rich.

E. These monopolies did not last. In the eighteenth century, a French official succeeded in smuggling nutmeg and clove seedlings out of the islands and planting them in French colonies in the Indian Ocean. Once the plants were grown in several regions, supply increased and prices fell. Spices gradually changed from luxuries into everyday goods, available to ordinary households across Europe and beyond.

F. The legacy of the spice trade remains visible today. Many cuisines around the world reflect centuries of exchange: chilli peppers, originally from the Americas, spread so rapidly through Asia after the sixteenth century that they are now central to many dishes that are thought of as traditional. Spices from Asia, in turn, became essential in the cooking of parts of Africa, Europe and the Caribbean. Port cities that grew rich on the trade still contain warehouses, merchants' houses and markets that date from that era, and some of these now attract large numbers of tourists.

G. Today, the global spice market is worth billions of dollars, and much of the production still comes from small farms. Many growers earn little, partly because prices can change dramatically from one year to the next. Some cooperatives are now trying to help farmers by selling directly to foreign buyers, an approach that, in a sense, echoes the old ambition of cutting out the intermediaries. Others are developing their own brands or processing spices locally, so that more of the final price stays in the growing regions.

script: Good evening. I'm Dr Nadia Kerr, and for the past two years I've led a study testing social robots in three care homes.
Let me start with what these robots are. They're not the human-shaped machines you see in films. Ours was about the size of a cat, and it could talk, play music and recognise faces.
They were never intended to replace care staff. Their purpose was to keep residents company and encourage conversation during quiet periods, especially in the evenings.
Before the trial, we expected the residents to be the most suspicious. In fact, it was the staff who had the most doubts, mainly because they worried about extra work.
The residents' favourite feature wasn't the conversation, which they found rather limited, but the music quizzes. Some groups played them every afternoon.
We measured loneliness using questionnaires. Overall, scores improved slightly, but the biggest effect was on residents who already had some interest in technology.
One surprise was that the robots encouraged residents to talk to each other more. They'd discuss the robot's strange answers over lunch.
There were problems too. The robots struggled to understand strong regional accents, and background noise in the lounge made this worse.
Families had mixed reactions. Some felt it was undignified for their parents to talk to a machine, while others were pleased that their relatives seemed happier.
Cost is another issue. Each robot cost about the same as two months of a part-time worker's wages, so we don't think care homes should buy them without careful thought.
Our next step is to test whether the robots can help residents with memory exercises, which we'll begin in the spring.

paragraphs: A. Across much of the world, populations are ageing rapidly. In many countries the number of people over eighty is expected to double within a few decades, while the number of working-age adults available to care for them is growing slowly or even shrinking. This imbalance has encouraged governments and technology companies to ask whether robots might take on some of the work currently done by human carers, either in care homes or in people's own houses. Supporters also point out that many older people would prefer to remain in their own homes for as long as possible, and that technology might make this easier.

B. Japan has been a pioneer in this field. Since the early 2000s, Japanese researchers have developed robots that can help lift patients from beds, guide residents through exercise sessions and act as companions. Some of these machines resemble animals rather than people; one well-known example takes the form of a baby seal, which responds to touch and sound. Designers chose this shape partly because people have fewer fixed expectations about how a seal should behave than about how a dog or cat should, so the robot's limitations are less noticeable.

C. Evidence about the benefits is encouraging but limited. Small studies have reported that companion robots can reduce agitation among people with dementia and improve their mood. However, many of these studies have involved only a few dozen participants and have lasted a few weeks, so it is difficult to know whether the effects would continue over time or simply reflect the novelty of a new object in the room. Researchers are now calling for larger and longer trials.

D. Lifting robots address a different problem. Moving patients is one of the main causes of back injuries among care workers, and machines that can take some of the strain could make the job safer. Yet in practice, such robots have been adopted slowly. They are expensive, take up space in small rooms and often take longer to use than a trained human, which matters in homes where staff are already under severe time pressure. Some homes have found ceiling-mounted lifting systems, which are much simpler machines, more practical.

E. Ethical questions have also been raised. Critics worry that robots could be used as an excuse to reduce human contact, leaving older people more isolated rather than less. Others are concerned about privacy, since many devices collect video and audio data. There is also the question of honesty: if a person with dementia believes a robot animal is alive, is it acceptable to allow that belief to continue? Opinions among carers and families differ considerably.

F. Supporters respond that the comparison should not be between robots and ideal human care, but between robots and the care that is actually available. In many places, staff shortages mean that residents spend long hours with little stimulation. From this perspective, a machine that encourages conversation or movement may be better than nothing, provided that it supplements human care rather than replacing it. They also note that robots do not become tired or impatient, and can repeat the same game or conversation as often as a resident wishes.

G. Most researchers now believe that the greatest potential lies not in replacing carers but in reducing the routine tasks that take up so much of their time, such as recording information or checking rooms at night. If technology can handle these tasks, staff may be able to spend more time on the personal interaction that machines cannot provide. Whether this happens, however, depends less on the technology itself than on how organisations decide to use the time it saves.

paragraphs: A. Long before the first powered aeroplane left the ground, people were experimenting with objects that could fly. The kite is one of the oldest of these. Historical records suggest that kites were flown in China at least two thousand years ago, made from silk or paper stretched over bamboo frames. From China, kite flying spread across Asia, where it became part of many festivals, and eventually reached Europe, where it became popular around the seventeenth century, mainly as a children's pastime. In some Asian countries, kite flying is still a major public event, attracting thousands of participants every year.

B. A kite stays in the air because of a balance between several forces. As wind flows over and under the angled surface, it creates lift, which pushes the kite upwards, and drag, which pushes it backwards. The line held by the flier provides tension, preventing the kite from simply blowing away. If the angle is too steep, drag increases and the kite falls; if it is too shallow, there is not enough lift to keep it up. A tail is often added to keep the kite stable, especially in gusty conditions, because it keeps the nose of the kite pointing into the wind.

C. Kites have frequently been used for serious purposes. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, meteorologists attached thermometers and other instruments to kites to measure conditions high above the ground. Some weather stations continued to use kites in this way until balloons and, later, aircraft took over the task. Kites were also used to lift cameras, producing some of the earliest aerial photographs, including views of cities taken after major disasters.

D. Perhaps the most important contribution of kites, however, was to the development of aviation. Several pioneers of flight used large kites to test ideas about wing shapes and control. The Wright brothers, for example, flew a large kite in 1899 to try out a method of twisting the wings to control the direction of flight, a technique that later became part of their successful aircraft. Without these cheap and relatively safe experiments, the first powered flights might have taken considerably longer to achieve.

E. In the twentieth century, kites briefly found military uses. Some navies used large kites to lift observers high above ships, allowing them to see much further, while others used them as targets for gunnery practice. These roles largely disappeared as aircraft and radar developed, and the kite returned mainly to the world of sport and leisure, where new materials such as nylon and carbon fibre made kites lighter and stronger than ever.

F. Recently, however, engineers have begun to look at kites again, this time as a source of energy. Winds at higher altitudes are stronger and more consistent than those near the ground, but building tall towers to reach them is expensive. Large kites tethered to the ground could, in theory, capture this energy, either by pulling on a cable that drives a generator or by carrying small turbines. Several companies are testing prototypes, although none has yet proved that the technology can compete on price with conventional wind turbines. Supporters argue that kite systems need far less material than towers, which could make them attractive in remote locations.

G. Kites are also being used to reduce fuel consumption at sea. A few cargo ships have been fitted with giant kites that fly far above the deck and help to pull the vessel along. Early trials suggest that the savings can be significant in the right wind conditions. Engineers are also studying whether similar systems could help fishing boats and even large passenger ferries. For a technology that is thousands of years old, the kite may still have a surprising future.

paragraphs: A. After water, tea is the most widely consumed drink in the world. Billions of cups are drunk every day, from the sweet, milky tea of South Asia to the bitter green teas of Japan and the mint tea of North Africa. Yet all these drinks derive from a single species, Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub that originated in the region where present-day China, Myanmar and India meet. The enormous variety of flavours comes from differences in climate, soil, harvesting and, above all, processing.

B. According to Chinese tradition, tea was first used as a medicine. Early texts describe it as a remedy for tiredness and poor digestion, and it was often boiled with other ingredients such as ginger or salt. Tea was pressed into hard cakes for storage and transport, and pieces were broken off when needed. Over many centuries, it became a drink valued for its own flavour. By the time of the Tang dynasty, more than a thousand years ago, tea drinking had spread across Chinese society, and a famous book devoted entirely to the cultivation and preparation of tea had been written.

C. From China, tea travelled along trade routes and with Buddhist monks, who valued it because it helped them stay awake during long periods of meditation. In Japan, monks brought back tea seeds and new methods of preparation, and over time a formal tea ceremony developed. This ceremony, with its precise movements and emphasis on calm and respect, is less about drinking tea than about creating a moment of shared attention between host and guests. Every detail, from the choice of bowl to the flowers in the room, is carefully considered.

D. Tea reached Europe in the early seventeenth century, carried by Dutch traders. At first it was expensive and drunk mainly by the wealthy, sometimes from tiny cups imported from China. In Britain, high taxes made it a target for smugglers, and for a period more tea may have entered the country illegally than legally. When taxes were sharply reduced in the late eighteenth century, tea became affordable for ordinary families and soon became a national habit.

E. The demand for tea had far-reaching consequences. To reduce dependence on Chinese supplies, British companies established large plantations in India and later in Sri Lanka and East Africa. These plantations transformed landscapes, replacing forests with neat rows of bushes, and relied on large numbers of workers, many of whom laboured in harsh conditions for very low wages. In Sri Lanka, tea replaced coffee as the main plantation crop after a disease destroyed many coffee farms in the nineteenth century. The effects of this history can still be seen in the economics of tea-growing regions today.

F. Scientific interest in tea has focused on its possible health benefits. Tea contains caffeine, though usually less than coffee, as well as a group of compounds called polyphenols. Herbal infusions such as camomile, often called tea, do not come from the tea plant and contain no caffeine. Some studies have linked regular tea drinking with a lower risk of heart disease, but researchers caution that tea drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in other ways, such as diet and lifestyle, which makes cause and effect difficult to establish.

G. Today, the tea industry faces new challenges. Climate change is affecting rainfall patterns in major growing regions, and higher temperatures can alter the flavour of the leaves. Some producers have responded by planting shade trees among their bushes and experimenting with more heat-tolerant varieties. At  the same time, consumers in many countries are showing growing interest in speciality teas and in where and how their tea is produced. Whether this interest will lead to better conditions for workers remains to be seen.

script: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Volcano Visitor Centre. I'm Marco, one of the geologists here, and I'm going to talk about why so many people choose to live near volcanoes.
It may seem strange, but around eight hundred million people worldwide live within a hundred kilometres of an active volcano.
The main attraction is the soil. Volcanic ash breaks down into soil that's rich in minerals such as potassium and phosphorus, which plants need.
However, fresh ash isn't immediately fertile. It can take decades, or even centuries, before it turns into good soil, and that depends largely on rainfall.
On our island, the slopes are famous for grapes. Local farmers grow vines in small holes dug in the ash, surrounded by low stone walls that protect them from the wind.
Volcanoes bring other benefits too. Hot springs attract tourists, and some countries use underground heat to produce electricity.
Of course, there are risks. Here, the greatest danger isn't lava, which usually moves slowly, but clouds of hot gas and ash that can travel downhill very fast.
The volcano is monitored constantly. Instruments measure small earthquakes and changes in the shape of the ground, which can swell before an eruption.
If an eruption is expected, residents receive a text message, and evacuation routes are marked with green signs.
People often ask whether eruptions can be predicted precisely. The honest answer is no. Scientists can warn that one is likely, but not say exactly when.
After the talk, do visit our simulator room, where you can feel what a small earthquake is like. It's suitable for children over eight.

paragraphs: A. Volcanoes are among the most destructive forces on Earth, yet they have also created some of its most productive landscapes. Around the world, from the slopes of Mount Etna in Sicily to the rice terraces of Java, communities have farmed volcanic land for thousands of years, often producing far more food per hectare than farmers on neighbouring land. Understanding why requires looking beneath the surface, at how volcanic material gradually becomes soil and what makes that soil different from soils formed in other ways.

B. When a volcano erupts, it may release lava, which cools into solid rock, and ash, made of tiny fragments of rock and glass. Ash is the more important of the two for agriculture. Because its particles are small and contain minerals that weather easily, ash can develop into fertile soil relatively quickly, especially in warm, wet climates. Lava flows, by contrast, may remain bare rock for centuries before plants can establish themselves, although mosses and lichens are often the first to appear.

C. The soils that form from volcanic ash have several useful properties. They tend to hold water well while still allowing excess water to drain away, and they are often rich in nutrients such as phosphorus and potassium. They also contain a high proportion of organic matter, because certain minerals in the ash bind to decaying plant material and slow its decomposition. As a result, volcanic soils can store large quantities of carbon, a fact that has attracted the attention of climate scientists.

D. Nevertheless, volcanic soils are not uniformly fertile. In some cases, the same minerals that hold organic matter also lock up phosphorus, making it difficult for plants to absorb. Farmers in parts of Japan and New Zealand have had to add large amounts of fertiliser to overcome this problem. In dry regions, ash weathers slowly, and young volcanic soils may be thin and stony for many generations. In very wet climates, heavy rainfall can also wash nutrients out of volcanic soils over long periods, gradually reducing their fertility.

E. The benefits of volcanic land come at a price. Eruptions can bury fields, destroy buildings and contaminate water supplies. Even small amounts of ash can damage crops and harm livestock that eat contaminated grass. Ash can also be carried hundreds of kilometres by the wind, affecting regions far from the volcano itself. Yet many farmers return to their land after eruptions, partly because the soil remains valuable and partly because of deep attachment to family land. Surveys in several countries have found that residents often underestimate the risks, particularly when the last major eruption took place before they were born.

F. Monitoring has greatly improved the safety of people living near volcanoes. Scientists use networks of instruments to detect small earthquakes, measure gases released from vents and track tiny changes in the shape of the ground. Satellites can now detect ground movement of just a few millimetres. These methods have allowed authorities to evacuate thousands of people before major eruptions, although forecasts are still uncertain, and false alarms can reduce public trust in future warnings. In some places, local residents are trained to report unusual signs, such as changes in the smell of springs or the behaviour of animals.

G. Increasingly, planners argue that living with volcanoes requires more than scientific monitoring. Clear communication, practised evacuation plans and land-use rules that keep homes out of the most dangerous valleys are all considered essential. For communities that depend on volcanic soils, the challenge is to make use of the land's riches while accepting that, sooner or later, the mountain will erupt again. Some regions now include volcanic risk in school lessons, so that children grow up knowing what to do.
